title: Finite subsets of rational modules lie in finite-dimensional submodules
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and $H$ an affine group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] over $k$. A rational $H$-module is a $k$-vector space $V$ with a $k$-linear coaction $\rho_V:V\to V\otimes_k k[H]$ satisfying $(\rho_V\otimes1)\rho_V=(1\otimes\Delta)\rho_V$ and $(1\otimes\epsilon)\rho_V=1_V$, where $\Delta,\epsilon$ are the comultiplication and counit of the coordinate Hopf algebra; $V^H=\{v:\rho_V(v)=v\otimes1\}$. For every finite subset $S\subset V$ there is a finite-dimensional $k$-subspace $W\subset V$ containing $S$ with $\rho_V(W)\subset W\otimes_k k[H]$. Thus $W$ is a rational submodule with the restricted coaction. No finite-dimensionality hypothesis on $V$ is required.

source.place: Proposition 4.7 and Corollary 4.8, printed pp.86--87: every rational representation is a filtered union of its finite-dimensional subrepresentations.

proof.text: Put $A=k[H]$. By [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-free], choose a $k$-basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of $A$, without requiring $I$ finite. By the basis definition [def-weil-pbc-free-module], the coefficient of $e_j$ defines a linear map $\lambda_j:A\to k$ with $\lambda_j(e_i)=\delta_{ji}$: addition and scalar multiplication add and multiply the unique basis coefficients. All basis expansions have finite support.

source.place: Proposition 4.7, printed p.86, and Corollary 4.8: coefficient comparison in equation (26).

proof.text: For any $k$-vector space $M$, each $t\in M\otimes_k A$ determines a unique finitely supported family $(m_i)_{i\in I}$ with $t=\sum_{i\in I}m_i\otimes e_i$; write $J=\{i:m_i\ne0\}$ for its finite support. Indeed, the pure tensors generate the tensor product [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]; expand the second factor of each of finitely many pure tensors in the basis [def-weil-pbc-free-module], then distribute and collect coefficients. The bilinear rule $m\otimes a\mapsto\lambda_j(a)m$ induces a linear map $E_j^M:M\otimes_k A\to M$ by the tensor universal property. Applying it to the expression gives $E_j^M(t)=m_j$ (zero outside $J$), proving uniqueness. The unit identification $M\otimes_k k\to M$ sends $m\otimes x$ to $xm$, with inverse $m\mapsto m\otimes1$. Reassociation sends $(m\otimes a)\otimes b$ to $m\otimes(a\otimes b)$, with the reverse formula as inverse. Iterating the universal property defines these maps; their composites fix every pure tensor, hence are identities because pure tensors generate.

source.place: Proposition 4.7, printed p.86, and Corollary 4.8: coefficient comparison in equation (26).

proof.text: For each $s\in S$, apply step 2 to write $\rho_V(s)=\sum_{i\in J_s}v_{s,i}\otimes e_i$ with $J_s$ finite. Let $W$ be the span of the finite family of all $v_{s,i}$ for $s\in S$ and $i\in J_s$. Thus $W$ is finite-dimensional by [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace], since these vectors span it by definition. Applying the counit identity to the displayed expansion gives $s=\sum_{i\in J_s}\epsilon(e_i)v_{s,i}$, so $S\subset W$. If $S$ is empty, this construction gives $W=0$.

source.place: Proposition 4.7, printed p.86, and Corollary 4.8: coefficient comparison in equation (26).

proof.text:
Fix $s\in S$ and $j\in J_s$. Coassociativity at $s$, after reassociating the triple tensor product, says
$$\sum_{i\in J_s}\rho_V(v_{s,i})\otimes e_i=\sum_{i\in J_s}v_{s,i}\otimes\Delta(e_i).$$
Apply the linear map $v\otimes a\otimes b\mapsto\lambda_j(b)(v\otimes a)$, furnished by the tensor universal property [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. The left side becomes $\rho_V(v_{s,j})$ and the right side becomes
$$\rho_V(v_{s,j})=\sum_{i\in J_s}v_{s,i}\otimes c_{i,j},\qquad c_{i,j}=(\mathrm{id}_A\otimes\lambda_j)\Delta(e_i)\in A,$$
where $A\otimes_k k$ is identified with $A$ by $a\otimes x\mapsto xa$. This explicitly puts the coaction of each spanning vector in the image of $W\otimes_k A$. Linearity therefore puts $\rho_V(W)$ in this image. This is Milne's equation (26), with its last two coefficient indices collected into $c_{i,j}$.

source.place: Proposition 4.7, printed p.86, and Corollary 4.8: coefficient comparison in equation (26).

proof.text: Write $\iota:W\hookrightarrow V$ for the inclusion. The map $\iota\otimes\mathrm{id}_A$ is injective, directly by step 2: if $t=\sum_i w_i\otimes e_i$ maps to zero, applying $E_j^V$ gives $\iota(w_j)=0$, hence every $w_j=0$ and $t=0$. Applying this argument twice also shows that $\iota\otimes\mathrm{id}_A\otimes\mathrm{id}_A$ is injective: first tensor the injective map $\iota\otimes\mathrm{id}_A$ with $A$, using exactly the same coefficient test. The coefficient maps exist by [def-weil-pbc-free-module] and [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]; no finite-dimensionality of $V$ or $A$ is used.

source.place: Proposition 4.7, printed p.86, and Corollary 4.8: coefficient comparison in equation (26).

proof.text: Step 4 and injectivity in step 5 define a unique $k$-linear map $\rho_W:W\to W\otimes_k A$ satisfying $(\iota\otimes\mathrm{id}_A)\rho_W=\rho_V\iota$: take the unique preimage of $\rho_V(w)$ for each $w$, and uniqueness proves additivity and homogeneity. Composing the two sides of the desired coassociativity identity for $\rho_W$ with $\iota\otimes\mathrm{id}_A\otimes\mathrm{id}_A$ gives respectively $(\rho_V\otimes\mathrm{id}_A)\rho_V\iota$ and $(\mathrm{id}_V\otimes\Delta)\rho_V\iota$. They are equal by the assumed coassociativity of $\rho_V$; injectivity gives the identity for $\rho_W$. Likewise $\iota(\mathrm{id}_W\otimes\epsilon)\rho_W=(\mathrm{id}_V\otimes\epsilon)\rho_V\iota=\iota$, and injectivity of $\iota$ gives the counit identity. These commutations follow on $w\otimes a$ from the tensor universal property [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. Hence $W$, already finite-dimensional and containing $S$, is a rational submodule with the restricted coaction. The argument includes $W=0$.
